passage: Last year, in Class 6, Hansa and I started the Sketch Squad. At first it was just us two drawing horses at break, and then three more girls who liked drawing joined. We had a secret sign, two fingers tapping the desk, and we always sat on the back bench by the window. After a while we made a rule: you had to show a drawing to join. When Meenu asked, "Zainab, can I sit with you?" I said, "Show us a drawing first." She didn't have one, so she went away. I felt a bit strange saying it, but it also felt good to have our own group.

qa.q: What was the Sketch Squad's secret sign?
qa.a: Two fingers tapping the desk.

qa.q: What mixed feelings did Zainab have about the rule?
qa.a: She felt a bit strange turning Meenu away, but she also enjoyed having a special group of their own.

qa.q: What could Zainab try to keep the shared interest without shutting people out?
qa.a: Invite newcomers to draw something with them right there, instead of asking for a drawing before they can sit.

qa.q: How might Meenu have felt walking away?
qa.a: She likely felt left out and unsure whether she would ever fit in with that group.

grounding: It shows a friend group forming around a shared interest and setting a boundary for who can join.

passage: Class teacher's note, Minakshi, Class 5. This month the class has split into clear groups. Pooja and four others call themselves "the Football Five." They wear their socks pulled up high, even on non-games days, and eat lunch in a circle facing inward. When a new boy stood near their circle, Pooja said, "Only players sit here," though she did move her bag for him later. The groups seem to give the children confidence. Next week I will mix the project teams so every group also works with others.

qa.q: What do the Football Five do with their socks?
qa.a: They wear them pulled up high, even on non-games days.

qa.q: Why might Pooja have moved her bag for the new boy later?
qa.a: She may have felt a little bad about her first words and wanted to include him despite the group rule.

qa.q: What is sensible about Minakshi's plan to mix the project teams?
qa.a: It keeps the confidence friend groups give while making sure children also work with people outside their circle.

qa.q: What is it like for the new boy near the circle?
qa.a: He probably feels on the outside at first, and the moved bag may be a small sign he could be let in.

grounding: It shows, in a teacher's note, a clique with shared markers and an in-group boundary.

passage:
Dear Diary,
Today Vidya finally asked me to sit with the Bookworms at lunch!! There are four of them, and they've read every mystery book in the library. They have their own words, like "cliffy" for a cliffhanger. I didn't know half of them. I nodded anyway. When Gauri from my old bench waved, I pretended I didn't see. I felt bad about that. But when Vidya said, "You're one of us now, Irawati," I felt warm all over. Tomorrow I'll bring my mystery book so they know I'm a real Bookworm. 📚

qa.q: What word do the Bookworms use for a cliffhanger?
qa.a: They say "cliffy" for a cliffhanger.

qa.q: Why did Irawati feel bad after ignoring Gauri?
qa.a: Irawati felt guilty, knowing that pretending not to see an old friend was unkind, even while wanting badly to fit in with the new group.

qa.q: What small step could Irawati take tomorrow?
qa.a: Wave back or say hi to Gauri too, showing that Irawati can belong to the Bookworms without dropping old friends.

qa.q: How might Gauri experience Irawati pretending not to see Gauri?
qa.a: Gauri may feel hurt and confused, wondering if a friend has been lost to the new group.

grounding: It shows a child joining a clique with its own shared words and interests, and the pull away from old friends.

passage: In the hill town of Kalimpong, Dolma and three girls from Class 6 called themselves the Kite Club. Every lunch break they sat on the same wall, flying paper kites and trading strings. They had a special three-tap handshake. When Gopika, new in school, wandered over holding a kite, Dolma said, 'This wall is only for the Club.' Gopika's face dropped. One of the girls whispered, 'She has a good kite, though.' Dolma hesitated, then said, 'Maybe tomorrow. We have to vote.' Gopika walked back slowly to the steps, still holding her kite.

qa.q: What did the girls call their group?
qa.a: They called themselves the Kite Club.

qa.q: What might Dolma be feeling when she hesitates?
qa.a: She seems torn between keeping the club special and knowing Gopika shares their interest and might fit in.

qa.q: What could the Kite Club do to be fairer to newcomers?
qa.a: They could invite interested children to join for a day, so the group keeps its fun without shutting people out.

qa.q: What is it like for Gopika to be turned away from the wall?
qa.a: It likely feels lonely and hurtful to be new and kept outside a group that shares her own interest.

grounding: Illustrates children forming a clique around a shared interest with clear in-group boundaries.

passage: At Lincoln Elementary in Chicago, the Sketch Squad ate lunch at the table by the window. Dalia had started it: five kids who drew comics and swapped markers. They had their own rule: no drawing sports. When Jamal sat down with a football doodle, a boy said, 'That's not Squad stuff.' Jamal looked at his drawing, then crumpled it. Dalia felt a twist in her stomach. 'He can draw what he wants,' she muttered, but the others were already laughing about a comic. Jamal moved to the next table, sketchbook under his arm.

qa.q: Where did the Sketch Squad eat lunch?
qa.a: They ate at the table by the window.

qa.q: What does Dalia's twist in her stomach suggest?
qa.a: It suggests she felt uneasy or guilty that her group's rule was excluding Jamal.

qa.q: What could Dalia do next time the group shuts someone out?
qa.a: She could speak up more clearly or suggest changing the rule, since she started the group.

qa.q: How might Jamal see the Sketch Squad after this?
qa.a: He may see them as unfriendly and feel that the group cares more about its rules than about people.

grounding: Shows children forming a friend group with shared interests and in-group rules, in the United States.

passage: In the school canteen, the tables had quietly sorted themselves. The cricket boys sat by the window, the singers near the door. Hafsa, eleven, and three friends had started the Sketch Squad: they sat at the corner table, drew in the same spiral notebooks and had a rule that you had to show one drawing a week. When Jatin wandered over with his tray, one of them said, "Only Sketch Squad here." Hafsa looked at him. "Do you draw?" He shrugged. "Bit." She pushed a pencil towards him. "Show us one on Monday, then."

qa.q: What rule did the Sketch Squad have?
qa.a: You had to show one drawing a week.

qa.q: What might Hafsa have been thinking when she asked Jatin "Do you draw?"
qa.a: She seemed curious and open, wanting to keep the group about drawing while giving him a fair chance.

qa.q: How could the Sketch Squad keep its identity without being unkind?
qa.a: Keep the group about the shared interest, and let anyone who draws try out, as Hafsa did.

qa.q: What is it like for Jatin to be told "Only Sketch Squad here"?
qa.a: He probably feels awkward and a bit shut out, until Hafsa gives him a way in.

grounding: Shows a friend group forming around a shared interest, with boundaries on who belongs.

passage: I'm Tushar, and I sit behind Lalremsiami in Class 6. Since the summer holidays, she and three girls have become a crew. They practise the same dance steps at lunch, wear matching purple hair clips, and have a secret handshake that ends with a finger snap. When another girl tried the handshake, Lalremsiami said kindly but firmly, "It's only for the crew." I don't know if she meant to leave people out. She just seems really happy with them. The four of them laugh at jokes the rest of us don't get.

qa.q: What do the girls wear to match?
qa.a: Purple hair clips.

qa.q: What might Lalremsiami be feeling about her crew?
qa.a: She seems happy and proud to belong to a close group with shared steps and signs.

qa.q: What could Lalremsiami do if another girl wants to join?
qa.a: Explain what the crew does and maybe invite her to learn the dance, rather than just saying no.

qa.q: How might the girl who tried the handshake feel?
qa.a: She might feel left out and embarrassed when told it's only for the crew.

grounding: Shows a friend group forming with shared interests and in-group signs, seen by a classmate.

passage: First Saturday of the holidays: Swati, ten, and her neighbour Uma spotted a kingfisher by the canal and decided to start a Bird Watchers Club. Second week: they had made paper badges, a notebook, and a secret code for each bird. Three other kids joined. Fourth week: when a boy who laughed at them wanted to join, Uma said, "Members have to know ten birds." Swati hesitated. "Let's teach him five first," she said. The club voted, and he got a trial week.

qa.q: What bird did Swati and Uma spot by the canal?
qa.a: A kingfisher.

qa.q: Why did Swati hesitate when Uma set the ten-birds rule?
qa.a: She felt torn between protecting the club and being fair to the boy.

qa.q: Which choice worked, and why?
qa.a: The trial week, because it kept the club's shared interest while giving the boy a fair chance.

qa.q: How might the boy feel about getting a trial week?
qa.a: Relieved and maybe a bit surprised, since he had laughed at them before.

grounding: Shows two children forming a club around a shared interest and deciding who can belong over several weeks.

passage: Ankita Dadi settled on the swing with Devika. "In class five, beta, four of us called ourselves the Tamarind Gang. We ate tamarind under one tree at lunch. We had a secret whistle, and only people who could climb the tree could join. When a new girl, Hema, asked to sit with us, I said, 'Climb first.' She couldn't. She ate alone for a week. We felt so important, having our own tree and our own whistle. But when my best friend moved away, the gang broke up, and Hema was the one who shared her tiffin with me." Devika pulled her feet up. "Did you ever say sorry to her?" Dadi smiled. "Much later."

qa.q: What did the Tamarind Gang use as their secret signal?
qa.a: A secret whistle.

qa.q: How did young Ankita and her friends feel about having their own tree and whistle?
qa.a: They felt important and proud to belong to a special group.

qa.q: Looking back, what could young Ankita have done when Hema asked to join?
qa.a: She could have let Hema sit with them even without climbing, instead of making the tree a test.

qa.q: How might Hema have felt eating alone that week?
qa.a: Hema likely felt lonely and left out after being turned away.

grounding: A grandmother remembers a school-age clique with a secret whistle and a rule that kept a new girl out.

passage: Rain had kept the Class 6 boys indoors for three days, and the hostel common room was cramped. Mohit and his four friends had built a card-trading club in one corner. They had a password, "Blue Tiger," and a rule: only card collectors could sit on the mat. Parveen from Class 5 hovered at the edge holding a small stack of her own cards. "I collect too," she said. Mohit glanced at the others. Two shook their heads. "Password?" Mohit asked. Parveen didn't know it. Then Mohit remembered how he'd felt last term, outside another group. "Come. Password's Blue Tiger," he said, and the others grumbled.

qa.q: What was the card-trading club's password?
qa.a: "Blue Tiger."

qa.q: What was Mohit feeling when he remembered being outside another group?
qa.a: He felt a pang of sympathy, recalling how left out he'd been, which pulled him toward letting Parveen in.

qa.q: What could Mohit do to help his friends accept the change?
qa.a: He could explain that the club was about collecting cards and suggest that anyone who collects can join.

qa.q: How might the other boys see Mohit's choice?
qa.a: They may feel annoyed that he bent the rules without asking them, and worry their club is less special.

grounding: Kept indoors by rain, a boy's card club has a password and membership rule, and a new collector tests its boundary.

passage: At lunch in the Jayanagar school, Sunaina's group always sat by the water cooler. There were five of them, all with the same star sticker on their notebooks, because they drew comics together. They had their own words, like "inking" and "panelling," that nobody else used. Kunal came over with his tray. "Can I sit?" The girls looked at each other. "Do you draw?" Sunaina asked. He pulled out a notebook full of rockets. Sunaina studied it, then slid over. "No star yet," she said. "You have to make a comic first." Kunal grinned and grabbed a pencil.

qa.q: What was on all five of the group's notebooks?
qa.a: The same star sticker.

qa.q: What was Sunaina feeling as she studied Kunal's notebook?
qa.a: She seemed cautious and curious, weighing whether he really shared the group's interest.

qa.q: How could Sunaina's group keep its shared interest without shutting others out?
qa.a: They could keep welcoming anyone who wants to draw, as they did with Kunal, instead of treating the star as a wall.

qa.q: What is it like for Kunal to approach the group?
qa.a: He is probably nervous at first, then relieved and excited when his rockets earn him a place.

grounding: An urban comics-drawing clique with its own stickers and words weighs whether a newcomer can join.

passage:
"We should start a club," Rukmini said at recess, flicking through her sketchbook.

"A drawing club," said Leela. "Only people who draw every day."

"And we meet under the neem tree at lunch."

"What about Ananya? She wants to join."

Rukmini frowned. "She only draws hearts."

"That's still drawing."

"Fine. But she has to bring her own pencils."

"And we need a name."

"The Sketch Squad."

"And a rule: no telling anyone our secret signal."

Leela giggled. "What's our secret signal?"

Rukmini tapped her pencil twice on her book. "This."

qa.q: Where does the club meet?
qa.a: They meet under the neem tree at lunch.

qa.q: How did Rukmini feel about Ananya joining?
qa.a: Rukmini was unsure and a bit reluctant, because Ananya only draws hearts.

qa.q: How could a teacher help the club stay welcoming?
qa.a: A teacher could encourage them to keep their shared interest while letting anyone who likes drawing join.

qa.q: How might Ananya feel if she were left out?
qa.a: Ananya would likely feel hurt and excluded.

grounding: Two children form a drawing club with shared interests, rules and a secret signal that marks who is in the group.

passage:
The summer I was ten, the lane split into two gangs. There was the cricket gang, which I joined, and the cycle gang, which Gargi led.

We had rules. Cricket gang members wore caps backwards and met at the empty plot at five. Cycle gang members rode in a line and wouldn't let anyone walk with them.

For weeks, we didn't talk to them. It felt important, like being on a team.

Then Gargi's chain broke, and nobody in her gang knew how to fix it. I did. I fixed it, and she let me ride at the back.

Looking back, the gangs made us feel we belonged. But they also made us miss out on each other. I'm Kiran, and I still have that cap.

qa.q: What did cricket gang members do with their caps?
qa.a: They wore caps backwards.

qa.q: How did Kiran feel about being in the cricket gang?
qa.a: Kiran felt proud and included, as if being on a team was important.

qa.q: What could the children have done to belong without shutting others out?
qa.a: They could keep their groups but also play together sometimes, as when Kiran fixed Gargi's chain.

qa.q: How might Gargi see Kiran after the chain was fixed?
qa.a: Gargi was likely grateful and began to see Kiran as a friend, not a rival.

grounding: A child looks back on a summer when friend groups formed with shared interests and boundaries.

passage:
Teacher's note, after the Diwali break.

Varun and four friends have started calling themselves "the Dino Five". They sit together at lunch, share dinosaur cards, and have a secret handshake.

Today Arjun asked to join, and Varun said, "Only five. That's the rule." Arjun sat alone.

I spoke to Varun privately. I said it's fine to have close friends, but asked how he'd feel if he were Arjun. He was quiet, then said, "Maybe he can be the dinosaur expert." Tomorrow I'll check how lunch goes.

— Dilnaz

qa.q: What did Varun say when Arjun asked to join?
qa.a: He said, "Only five. That's the rule."

qa.q: How did Varun feel when Dilnaz asked how he'd feel if he were Arjun?
qa.a: Varun felt thoughtful and perhaps a little guilty, going quiet before suggesting a role for Arjun.

qa.q: How did Dilnaz handle the situation well?
qa.a: She spoke to Varun privately, accepted his friendships, and helped him think of Arjun's feelings.

qa.q: How might Arjun feel sitting alone?
qa.a: Arjun would likely feel hurt and left out.

grounding: A teacher notes a boy's friend group forming strict boundaries and helps him think about including another child.

passage:
Dear Diary, 14 April, Baisakhi holiday
Today the colony kids split up for real. Tanmay's lot say only people who can bowl fast are in the "Tigers". Urmila and I aren't fast, so we sat on the water tank and started our own group: the Comic Keepers. Rules: you must own at least one comic, you must bring snacks on Sundays, and no Tigers allowed. Urmila drew a badge. Ravi wanted to join, but he doesn't have any comics, so I said no. He walked off kicking stones. I felt a bit bad, but rules are rules. Tomorrow we meet at five.
Mohit

qa.q: What is the name of the group Mohit and Urmila started?
qa.a: The Comic Keepers.

qa.q: How did Mohit feel after saying no to Ravi?
qa.a: Mohit felt a bit bad and uneasy, but held on to the idea that rules are rules.

qa.q: What could Mohit and Urmila do so their club doesn't shut people out the way the Tigers did?
qa.a: They could relax the comic rule, for example lending Ravi one, so the club is about a shared interest rather than keeping people out.

qa.q: What is it like for Ravi to be turned away?
qa.a: Ravi feels rejected and hurt, kicking stones on the way out, much as Mohit and Urmila were shut out by the Tigers.

grounding: Illustrates children forming a club with shared interests and firm rules about who is in and who is out.
